title: Climate change projections using the IPSL-CM5 Earth System Model: from CMIP3 to CMIP5
problem: The paper addresses the limitations of previous climate models by developing an Earth System Model that integrates key biogeochemical processes like the carbon cycle, aerosols, and atmospheric chemistry, which were previously studied separately, to provide more comprehensive climate projections.
method: This paper presents the IPSL-CM5 Earth System Model, which couples physical climate components with interactive carbon cycle, chemistry, and aerosol models to simulate historical climate changes and project future climate under different CMIP5 socio-economic scenarios.
task: The task is to present the IPSL-CM5 Earth System Model and its use in simulating the long-term climate response to natural and anthropogenic forcings for historical and future scenarios as part of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project 5 (CMIP5).
innovation: This paper presents the IPSL-CM5 Earth System Model for CMIP5, detailing its new components including an interactive carbon cycle, comprehensive aerosols, and atmospheric chemistry, and analyzes its climate change projections under various historical and future socio-economic scenarios.

ORCHIDEE (ORganizing Carbon and Hydrology In Dynamic Ecosystems) is a land-surface model that simulates the energy and water cycles of soil and vegetation, the terrestrial carbon cycle, and the vegetation composition and distribution (Krinner et al. 2005).

The ocean and sea-ice component is based on NEMOv3.2 (Nucleus for European Modelling of the Ocean, Madec 2008), which includes OPA for the dynamics of the ocean, PISCES for ocean biochemistry, and LIM for sea-ice dynamics and thermodynamics.

The LMDZ5B version is characterized by a much better representation of the boundary layer and associated clouds, by a delay of several hours of the diurnal cycle of continental convection, and by a stronger and more realistic tropical variability. LMDZ5B is used within the IPSL-CM5B model.

The ocean and sea-ice component is based on NEMOv3.2 (Nucleus for European Modelling of the Ocean, Madec 2008), which includes OPA for the dynamics of the ocean, PISCES for ocean biochemistry, and LIM for sea-ice dynamics and thermodynamics.

The ocean and sea-ice component is based on NEMOv3.2 (Nucleus for European Modelling of the Ocean, Madec 2008), which includes OPA for the dynamics of the ocean, PISCES for ocean biochemistry, and LIM for sea-ice dynamics and thermodynamics.
The model uses a classical so-called hybrid σ – p coordinate in the vertical. The number of layers has been increased from 19 to 39 compared to the previous LMDZ4 version, with 15 levels above 20 km.

PISCES (Pelagic Interaction Scheme for Carbon and Ecosystem Studies) (Aumont and Bopp 2006) simulates the cycling of carbon, oxygen, and the major nutrients determining phytoplankton growth (phosphate, nitrate, ammonium, iron and silicic acid).

ORCHIDEE (ORganizing Carbon and Hydrology In Dynamic Ecosystems) is a land-surface model that simulates the energy and water cycles of soil and vegetation, the terrestrial carbon cycle, and the vegetation composition and distribution (Krinner et al. 2005).
For deep convection, the LMDZ5A version uses the "episodic mixing and buoyancy sorting" scheme originally developed by Emanuel (1991). LMDZ5A is used within the IPSL-CM5A model.

At Low Resolution (LR), the model has 96 × 95 points corresponding to a resolution of 3.75° × 1.875° in longitude and latitude respectively and at Medium Resolution (MR) the model has 144 x 143 points, corresponding to a resolution of 2.5° x 1.25°.

An important result for IPSL-CM5 is the very strong difference between the climate sensitivities obtained with IPSL-CM5A-LR and IPSL-CM5B-LR. While the climate sensitivity of IPSL-CM5A-LR (∆T (2CO2) ≈ 4.1K) lies in the upper part of the sensitivity range of the CMIP3 models, the sensitivity of IPSL-CM5B-LR (AT (2CO2) ≈ 2.6K) falls in the lower part (Meehl et al. 2007b).

As shown later in Sect. 4.2, the IPSL-CM5A-LR historical runs show a cold bias of about 1 K compared to present-day observations. This bias is due to the fact that during the tuning phase the oceanic model was far from equilibrium and the aerosols, volcanoes, and ozone forcings did not reach their final values.

The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) maximum is represented in Fig. 20 for different simulations from the IPSL-CM5A-LR and the IPSL-CM5A-MR models. This index represents the strength of the meridional circulation over the North Atlantic (30°S-80°N, 500 m-5,000 m) and the amount of ocean water sinking at depth in the North Atlantic.
